scenario: AITA for not hosting thanksgiving like I planned to | For about 50 years, my mom hosted all of her children and grandchildren for thanksgiving and Christmas Eve. She’s now gotten too old and asked us kids to take over the tradition. There are 4 of us so we just rotate. We’ve each hosted one holiday so far. This thanksgiving is my turn. We have never spent thanksgiving or Christmas Eve with my wife’s family. We’ve just never been as close to them plus they live all over the country. Well this year her mom and aunts decided to go to the Macy’s thanksgiving day parade. At first it was just a sister’s trip but then they decided to invite all their kids and grandkids to meet them up there. My wife really wants to go. She hasnt seen some of her aunts and cousins in years. Our daughter wants to go because it’s a “once in a lifetime event” (which i agree with). And I want to go. As soon as we decided to go I called my older brother to see what we should do about thanksgiving because I can’t host this year. He said our oldest sister is going to be pissed and i have to tell her myself. He wished me luck. So I call her and she is mad. She says she’ll probably have to end up hosting even though she is up next for Christmas and I’m being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. “Mom wouldn’t abandon thanksgiving to go to nyc” and went on about how sad mom will be that I’m doing this. I offered to pay for them to rent a spot and have it catered but she said that takes away from the close knit family vibe. My brother said his wife might be up for it but he didn’t sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can’t do it because she’s renovating her house. I do feel bad for backing out of my turn but I tried to offer up solutions and I also offered to host the next holiday—which my oldest sister said no to because it’s her turn and she’s been planning for it all year. Next up is my brother so I said me and him could maybe just swap thanksgivings if his wife is up for it. Am I in the wrong here?

If this is truly a once-in-a-lifetime experience for your wife and daughter, and it’s something they’ve been looking forward to, it might be reasonable to make an exception—especially if the alternative (hosting a traditional Thanksgiving) feels like a missed opportunity for them. 2. **Fairness and Rotation** - The rotation system was likely designed to share the burden of hosting evenly. By skipping your turn, you’re shifting the responsibility onto your sister, who may have already planned her holiday. This could feel unfair, especially if she’s been looking forward to hosting. - **Is it wrong to ask for a swap?** Not necessarily, but it depends on how your siblings respond. If your brother’s wife is willing to host, and your sister is open to swapping, that could be a fair compromise. However, if your sister is adamant about not changing the rotation (even for a one-time exception), you might need to accept that this year’s Thanksgiving won’t happen as planned. 3. **The "Close-Knit Family Vibe" Argument** - Your sister’s point—that renting a spot and catering takes away from the "close-knit family vibe"—is subjective. Neither approach is inherently "wrong," but it’s important to acknowledge that this is a clash of values. - **Is it wrong to suggest alternatives?** Not at all. You’re showing goodwill by offering solutions, but your sister’s refusal to compromise might reflect her attachment to the tradition. This doesn’t make you wrong; it just means you’re dealing with differing priorities. 4. **Your Mom’s Perspective** - Your sister’s comment about "Mom wouldn’t abandon Thanksgiving to go to NYC" is poignant. It’s possible your mom would have understood the significance of this trip, especially if it’s a rare chance for your wife and daughter to reconnect with their family. However, she might also have valued the tradition of gathering as a unit. - **Is it wrong to assume what your mom would want?** It’s tricky. You don’t know for sure, but if this trip holds deep meaning for your wife and daughter, it might be worth considering whether your mom would have encouraged them to seize the moment—even if it meant skipping the traditional gathering. 5. **Your Own Feelings** - You’re clearly torn. You feel bad about backing out of your turn, but you also want to support your wife and daughter. This is a tough spot, and it’s okay to feel conflicted. The fact that you’re offering solutions (like swapping with your brother or hosting next time) shows that you’re trying to be fair and considerate. ### **Where Do You Stand?** - **If you prioritize tradition and family unity**, you might feel that skipping Thanksgiving is disrespectful to your mom’s legacy and your siblings’ expectations. Hosting next year or finding another way to include everyone (even if it’s not in person) could be the right choice for you. - **If you prioritize your wife and daughter’s happiness and this once-in-a-lifetime opportunity**, you might feel that missing the trip would be a bigger regret than skipping Thanksgiving. In that case, you could frame it as a temporary deviation from the rotation, with the understanding that the tradition will continue in the future. - **If you see this as a middle ground**, you could propose a hybrid solution: for example, hosting a smaller, more intimate Thanksgiving for your immediate family (your wife, daughter, and maybe your brother and his wife) while acknowledging that your wife’s family is prioritizing their trip. ### **Final Thought:** There’s no universal "right" answer, but the most important thing is to approach this with honesty and empathy. You could: 1. **Acknowledge the conflict**—let your sister know you understand her feelings and that you’re trying to balance everyone’s needs. 2. **Offer a compromise**—if possible, suggest a way to include both the trip and the tradition (e.g., a smaller gathering later or a virtual connection for those who can’t be there). 3. **Accept that some things can’t be fixed**—if no solution satisfies everyone, it might be about managing expectations and moving forward. Ultimately, this is a test of how your family handles change and compromise. Your willingness to engage with the situation thoughtfully (even if it doesn’t resolve perfectly) shows that you care deeply about your family—whether that’s through tradition or new experiences. **My personal take?** It’s not inherently wrong to prioritize the trip, but it’s also not wrong to feel guilty about it. The key is to do what feels most authentic to your values while being mindful of how your choices affect others. You’re navigating a tough spot, and there’s no shame in that.
